cards.term: The Newfoundland fishing community
cards.def: Fisherfolk, mariners, and merchants from many nations crowded the Grand Banks off Newfoundland, swapping tales of Portuguese voyages, John Cabot's search, and Columbus's discovery.

cards.term: The characteristics of fifteenth-century European society
cards.def: Fifteenth-century Europe was isolated and backward, with about 90 percent of people living in scattered villages and working the land amid chronic food shortages and catastrophic disease.

cards.term: How Europe depended on Muslim middlemen
cards.def: Before the fifteenth century, western Europeans relied on Muslim merchants and mariners to bring the goods and learning of Asia and sub-Saharan Africa overland to Europe.

cards.term: The motives for European exploration
cards.def: Europeans explored to reach Asian riches directly without Muslim middlemen, gain gold and new markets and land, spread Christianity against Islam, and win glory for rival monarchs.

cards.term: The achievements that made the Age of Exploration possible
cards.def: Exploration rested on political nation-states, economic recovery after the Black Death, military armies and navies, and navigational technology such as caravels, lateen sails, and astrolabes.

cards.term: How the Black Death set the stage for expansion
cards.def: By killing so many Europeans, the Black Death eased population pressure and raised survivors' wealth, freeing capital for new technology, trade, and overseas ventures.

cards.term: How the Mediterranean Atlantic led to wider exploration
cards.def: Portuguese success on the Wine Islands with sugar and slave labor supplied profits, skills, and a plantation model that pushed exploration on to Africa, Asia, and the Americas.

cards.term: Why sugar plantations depended on slavery
cards.def: Because sugar required relentless planting, harvesting, and processing, planters turned to enslaved Africans as the cheapest and most controllable labor.

cards.term: How slavery developed along coastal West Africa
cards.def: Because strong West African states and deadly diseases blocked conquest, the Portuguese bargained with coastal rulers and bought enslaved Africans for Atlantic-island sugar plantations.

cards.term: The significance of Columbus's voyage
cards.def: Columbus's landfall linked two hemispheres that had developed separately for thousands of years, producing a world-changing encounter instead of the Asian trade route he expected.

cards.term: Why Spain conquered the Aztecs and Incas so quickly
cards.def: The Spanish won because of Indian allies who hated their unpopular rulers, divisions within the empires, smallpox epidemics, and Spanish firearms, steel weapons, and horses.

cards.term: The results of the conquest of Mexico
cards.def: The conquest destroyed the Aztec Empire, killed millions of Indians through war and disease, and made Mexico the wealthy center of Spain's American empire.

cards.term: Why disease was Spain's strongest weapon
cards.def: Because Native Americans had never encountered Eurasian diseases, virgin-soil epidemics of smallpox killed vast numbers and crippled resistance before and during conquest.

cards.term: How Spain governed its American empire
cards.def: Spanish monarchs soon replaced the independent conquistadors with an elaborate civil and church bureaucracy, so no colonial nobility could challenge royal authority.

cards.term: How American silver changed Spain and Europe
cards.def: American silver made Spain enormously rich and pushed Europe toward more capitalist economies and more centralized political authority, at the cost of many coerced Indian and African miners' lives.

cards.term: The elements of the Columbian Exchange
cards.def: The Americas gave the world maize, potatoes, squash, beans, tomatoes, and tobacco, while Europe and Africa brought horses, cattle, pigs, wheat, sugarcane, enslaved Africans, and smallpox and measles.

cards.term: What Protestant reformers criticized and taught
cards.def: Luther and Calvin attacked the Catholic Church's worldliness and corruption and taught that people were saved by divine grace alone and could read God's will in the Bible.

cards.term: How the Reformation shaped the colonization of America
cards.def: The Reformation turned European rivalry into religious war, so Catholic and Protestant powers treated colonies as outposts to defend their faith, and persecuted Protestants sought American refuges.

cards.term: Why Spain fortified Florida
cards.def: Spain founded St. Augustine to suppress French pirates, block French colonization, and keep Protestants away from the routes of its treasure fleets.

cards.term: Why England entered colonization late and then aggressively
cards.def: Barred from Spain's American preserve, English adventurers first fought religious wars and conquered Ireland, until fear of Spain and merchants' hunger for markets and land drove Elizabeth to colonize.

cards.term: Ireland as a model for English colonization
cards.def: England conquered Ireland before America, and veterans of the Irish campaigns brought its military, quasi-feudal methods and contempt for natives to Roanoke and the Chesapeake.

cards.term: Why Native leaders welcomed the first English colonists
cards.def: Native leaders such as Wingina tolerated the English because trade goods, weapons, and alliances with the newcomers might strengthen their own power.

cards.term: Why the Roanoke colony failed
cards.def: Historians blame Roanoke's failure on English leaders who demanded food while using violence against Wingina's people and on the Spanish Armada crisis that cut off the colony's supplies.

cards.term: How the European colonial empires differed
cards.def: The Spanish and French sent few settlers, ruled centrally, and worked to Christianize Indians, while England sent many settlers and made little missionary effort.

cards.term: England's position in the global race for empire by 1600
cards.def: By 1600 Portugal and Spain had built overseas empires, while England's failed experiments laid the groundwork for its renewed expansion in the seventeenth century.

cards.term: Why Chinese voyages did not precede Columbus to America
cards.def: Chinese leaders grounded Zheng He's treasure fleet and ended long-distance voyages, so China left no route to the Americas before Columbus.

cards.term: Why Mehmet II's conquest alarmed Europe
cards.def: Mehmet II's 1453 capture of Constantinople alarmed Europe economically and militarily because the Ottomans now controlled eastern Mediterranean trade routes.

cards.term: How financial techniques enabled expansion
cards.def: By the late fifteenth century, merchants and bankers used efficient money transfers and credit over long distances, providing capital for technology, trade, and colonial enterprises.

cards.term: How the Portuguese solved the Atlantic return problem
cards.def: Atlantic currents made returning from Africa nearly impossible, so Portugal became the first kingdom to solve it with caravels, lateen sails, and a sturdier Islamic astrolabe.

cards.term: What Portugal traded in West Africa
cards.def: Portugal traded textiles, raw and worked metal, cowry-shell currency, and beads for West African gold, ivory, malaguetta pepper, and slaves.

cards.term: Why sugar plantations kept moving west
cards.def: Sugar exhausted soil quickly, while the Black Death and Ottoman conquests cut Mediterranean labor and Balkan slave sources, pushing plantations to the Atlantic islands and West African slaves.

cards.term: Why Columbus's second voyage became colonization
cards.def: Gold rumors, a vulnerable Taino population lacking West African military power, and a healthy climate turned Columbus's second voyage into colonization rather than commerce.

cards.term: How Spaniards and Aztecs were similar
cards.def: Spaniards and Aztecs were both rural agricultural societies with urban merchants, specialized craftworkers, noble and priestly elites, tribute systems, and expansionist goals.

cards.term: Why the Aztecs were vulnerable
cards.def: The Aztecs lacked ocean navigation, metal tools and weapons, and firearms, and their young empire had not fully controlled central Mexico.

cards.term: Why the Taino population collapsed
cards.def: Within one generation Taino numbers collapsed through war, overwork, malnutrition, despair, and Eurasian diseases, as Spanish slavers also depopulated the Bahamas.

cards.term: How Europeans and Indians judged each other's dress
cards.def: Europeans saw Native nakedness as lust or innocence, while Native observers found Europeans' wool clothing and limited bathing barbaric; clothing marked a supposed civilized-savage boundary.

cards.term: How the Columbian Exchange reshaped the Caribbean
cards.def: Europeans likely carried syphilis home and brought horses, large dogs, oranges, lemons, figs, and bananas, while escaped hogs and rats overran Caribbean islands.

cards.term: How Indians lived under Spanish rule
cards.def: Indians often stayed on former Aztec and Inca farms, paid Spanish taxes, raised export livestock, and supplied coerced labor in mines beside Black slaves.

cards.term: How Spanish treasure and trade moved by 1600
cards.def: Potosí silver went by ship to Panama, overland across the Isthmus, then from the Caribbean to Spain, while an Acapulco expedition sailed yearly to the Philippines.

cards.term: Why first-contact sources must be read critically
cards.def: Accounts by Bernal Díaz in the 1560s and Bernardino de Sahagún's 1540s informants are later, partial, and shaped by the authors' positions and purposes.

cards.term: What de Soto's expedition did to the Southeast
cards.def: De Soto's men ravaged the Southeast from Florida to Texas, found no treasure, and hastened the shift from Mississippian chiefdoms to decentralized confederacies.

cards.term: Why Spain dominated the Americas in the sixteenth century
cards.def: Spain dominated the Americas for most of the sixteenth century because rival powers were absorbed in the religious upheaval of the Protestant Reformation.

cards.term: Why Catholic Church abuses provoked reform
cards.def: Between 1100 and 1500 church wealth, landholding, tithes, office fees, and political interference clashed with poorly educated priests and popular demands for assurance of salvation.

cards.term: How Catholic and Protestant views of salvation differed
cards.def: Catholic teaching stressed faith plus good works, sacraments, pilgrimages, and prayer, while Luther taught justification by faith alone, with good behavior following salvation.

cards.term: How the Reformation divided Europe
cards.def: Spain, Portugal, Ireland, and Italy stayed Catholic; England, Scotland, the Netherlands, Switzerland, and France had Calvinists; Germany and Scandinavia became largely Lutheran.

cards.term: How Henry VIII's Church of England compared with Catholicism
cards.def: Henry VIII made himself head of the Church of England after the pope refused an annulment but retained essentially Catholic teaching and ritual.

cards.term: How the English treated the Irish
cards.def: English colonizers portrayed Catholic Irish as savage and denied them land, offices, juries, testimony, trades, and weapons, a precedent for brutality toward savage peoples.

cards.term: What Gilbert's charter claimed
cards.def: Gilbert's 1578 charter covered American land not held by a Christian prince between Florida and Labrador, ignored Native possession, and envisioned feudal lords and free land for the poor.

cards.term: What Hakluyt said America offered England
cards.def: Hakluyt promoted North America for tropical commodities, attacks on Spain, a Northwest Passage, Protestantism, English markets, and relief for the poor and unemployed.

cards.term: Theories on the fate of the lost Roanoke colonists
cards.def: The fate of the lost Roanoke colonists remains unknown: they may have moved to Croatoan, joined Native communities, or been killed.

cards.term: What the chapter summary says enabled European expansion
cards.def: Europe's expansion was enabled by technology, new trade networks, financial techniques, and political centralization, while Native divisions and European diseases enabled Spanish conquest.
